title: Acharei Mot: live by them (Leviticus 18:5)
hook: "which if a man do, he shall live by them"; so saving a life overrides almost every law (Yoma 85b)

segments.voice: Yesterday in Acharei Mot, the Mishnah's condition: wrongs between people need their forgiveness. Your line was ask the person first. Did you say sorry to someone, without a but? Today, the end of the portion, and a rule about the rules. Day four hundred nine.

It's Saturday morning in an observant neighborhood. A man who wouldn't turn on a light switch on Shabbat, who walks to synagogue in the rain rather than drive, sees his neighbor collapse on the sidewalk. He pulls out his phone, calls an ambulance, and does everything the dispatcher tells him. Nobody who knows Jewish law would blink. In fact, they'd say he did exactly what the law requires. The reason goes back to a few words in Leviticus 18, and to a rabbi who read them very carefully.
screen: `A MAN COLLAPSES ON SHABBAT.` → `THE PHONE COMES OUT.` → `EXACTLY WHAT THE LAW REQUIRES.`

segments.voice: In the 1917 Jewish Publication Society translation, God's statutes and ordinances are the ones "which if a man do, he shall live by them." In the Talmud, the sages ask where we learn that saving a life overrides Shabbat. Several answers are offered, and the one left standing is Samuel's: he shall live by them, and not die by them. The commandments are for living. If keeping one would cost a life, the life comes first. Jewish law calls this pikuach nefesh. Nefesh is a life, a soul. Pikuach comes from a picture in the Mishnah: rubble falls on someone on Shabbat, and you don't know whether they're under it, or alive. You clear the rubble anyway. That clearing, uncovering, is pikuach. Even a doubt about danger to life is enough. There are limits. The Talmud names three things a person may not do even to save their own life: worship idols, commit murder, or commit certain forbidden sexual acts. Almost everything else gives way. Fasting on Yom Kippur, Shabbat, the food laws: a sick person may be required to set them aside. And the idea reaches into ordinary days. Maimonides counts keeping your body healthy as part of serving God, because you can't do much of anything if you're broken. Live by them. Not in spite of them.
screen: `HE SHALL LIVE BY THEM.` · `SAMUEL: AND NOT DIE BY THEM.` · `PIKUACH: CLEARING THE RUBBLE.` · `THREE LIMITS, AND A LONG REACH.` · then, large: `LIVE BY THEM.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look after your health today. Settle, and breathe, and notice your body. Where is it tired, tight, ignored? When did you last drink water, eat properly, sleep enough, walk outside, see a doctor about the thing you keep putting off? Choose one small thing your body needs today, and decide when you'll do it. Not as self-improvement. As taking care of a life. The bell holds the time.
Pikuach nefesh. Saving a life: the principle, drawn from live by them, that protecting life overrides almost every other commandment.
Your line: live by them. Today, do the one thing for your health that you've been putting off: book it, drink it, sleep it. Day four hundred nine.

howItsDone: Jewish law requires setting aside Shabbat, fasts and most other commandments to save a life or treat serious illness; observant doctors, nurses and volunteer ambulance crews work on Shabbat for this reason.

fork.reveal: clear it now, even on a doubt. that act of uncovering gives the principle its name: pikuach nefesh.

original.note: Hebrew: saving a life; literally uncovering a soul, from clearing rubble off someone.

trapdoor: what you thought: an emergency exception.
what it means: the commandments exist for life, so protecting life comes first.
what a scholar hears: Yoma 85b prefers Samuel's derivation from Leviticus 18:5; Mishnah Yoma 8:7 gives the rubble case; Sanhedrin 74a lists the three exceptions.
